transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-25
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Rivera (CTO - BlueFin), Sofia Chen (Infrastructure Lead), Alex Gomez (ML Eng)

Summary (auto): Technical deep dive on autoscaling strategies and capacity planning for BlueFin's production LLM endpoints. Covered burst policies, queueing, reserved GPU sizing, KV cache behavior, batching trade-offs, quantization impacts, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed next steps: send capacity worksheet, share security docs, run benchmarks.

Topics: autoscaling policy, burst capacity, queueing models, reserved GPUs, KV cache, batching, quantization, VPC private deployment, benchmark plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we wanted to do a deep dive on, on auto-scaling and capacity planning and, uh figure out how BlueFin wants to approach burst workloads versus steady-state, so I'll hand off to Priya to kick off the technical bits.
[00:14] Priya Nair: Yeah thanks Jordan. Hi Mark, Sofia, Alex. Quick agenda: we'll cover traffic profile assumptions, queueing models we use, reserved GPU sizing, burst policies and fallbacks, and then some notes on KV cache, batching, and quant, quantization, and then VPC/on-prem constraints.
[00:28] Mark Rivera: Sounds good. Just to set context, our current peak is about 1200 concurrent users hitting a chat endpoint, roughly 40 requests per second, but each request has variable length, average 450 tokens output, input avg 300 tokens, and we have occasional spikes up to 250 rps during reports.
[00:45] Alex Gomez: And for ML team, our latency SLO is 300 ms median for short requests, p95 we want under 800 ms, otherwise product complains. We're currently on a managed endpoint on another vendor but costs are high and cold start behavior is poor.
[00:58] Priya Nair: Cool. quick callout, some of the numbers matter a lot for the queueing model. Is the 40 rps steady or more bursty?
[01:05] Mark Rivera: It's more bursty, like 40 rps baseline, then 3x-6x spikes for 10-20 minutes around reports.
[01:11] Priya Nair: Got it. So Redwood's Dedicated product supports reserved GPUs for steady capacity plus burst pools. The model is: reserved pool handles guaranteed throughput, autoscaler maintains a buffer, and burst capacity can be pre-warmed or cold start depending on policy.
[01:26] Sofia Chen: When you say pre-warmed, do you mean we keep extra instances idle? That seems expensive.
[01:31] Priya Nair: Yeah this is the cost/latency tradeoff. Pre-warming means you pay a reserved or on-demand unit that's ready to accept traffic with warm KV cache and model loaded — near-zero cold-start penalty. If you allow cold scaling, we spin up additional workers when queue grows, which is cheaper but you see warmup latency. We also support soft-queueing with priority lanes so short requests don't get stuck behind long-running ones.
[01:54] Alex Gomez: Can you explain soft-queueing and priority lanes a bit more?
[01:57] Priya Nair: Sure. We use a multi-queue model: short-path lane for requests under X tokens and a long-path lane for longer ones. Requests are assigned based on estimated decode time; each lane has its own target concurrency. If long requests saturate long-lane, short-lane still gets isolated throughput. It's not perfect — estimates can be noisy — but reduces head-of-line blocking.
[02:18] Mark Rivera: How do you estimate decode time? We saw weird variability with different quant models.
[02:22] Priya Nair: We use historical tokens-per-second per model and per sequence-length bucket. There's a small prediction correction at runtime; sometimes tokenizer differences or model configs cause divergence, we see that in logs. There can be mis-reads, like K-V cache being spelled out K V cash in some logs, so we built heuristics to reconcile.
[02:38] Jordan Lee: (laughs) We've seen the kv-cache spelled a dozen ways in various transcripts.
[02:42] Sofia Chen: On KV cache — how much does it actually help for our usage? We have lots of multi-turn chat sessions and reuse prior context a lot.
[02:49] Priya Nair: KV caching is huge for multi-turn. If your sessions have prefixes or repeated system prompts, the KV cache avoids recomputing attention for the prefix. In practice we see 20-60% token cost reduction and lower latency on subsequent turns. But caching has memory footprint on the worker — more cached keys means fewer concurrent unique sessions per GPU. So cache policy interacts with reserved sizing.
[03:12] Alex Gomez: So if we enable aggressive KV cache, we'd need more GPU RAM or fewer concurrent sessions per GPU?
[03:17] Priya Nair: Exactly. It's a capacity tradeoff. We model session cardinality * average cache size to compute memory footprint. For BlueFin's average context length, our rough calc says enabling prefix KV cache for 70% of sessions increases per-session memory by ~1.6x, which reduces concurrency per 80GB GPU from ~28 sessions to ~18 sessions.
[03:38] Mark Rivera: That math is critical for reserved pool sizing. Do you provide a worksheet?
[03:41] Jordan Lee: Yes we'll send a capacity planning worksheet — that will let you plug in token distributions and session affinity to get recommended reserved GPU counts.
[03:50] Sofia Chen: What about batching? We've seen vendors do micro-batching to improve throughput but that hurts tail latency. How do you balance batching and p95?
[03:58] Priya Nair: Redwood's runtime supports adaptive batching — we batch up to a size limit and time-slice to keep latency under SLOs. There are two levers: max batch size and max batch wait (ms). For low-latency apis we keep max wait small (e.g., 8-12 ms) and smaller batch sizes. For throughput optimized workloads you can increase wait to 30-50 ms and larger batches. We also support priority batching where short requests bypass the batch or get their own mini-batches.
[04:23] Alex Gomez: And quantization — does 4-bit quant give similar latency improvements across models? We're evaluating q4_0 and q8-style profiles.
[04:30] Priya Nair: Quantization reduces memory footprint and can increase throughput on some kernels, but not all quant profiles behave the same. q4_0 often reduces memory the most and enables more concurrent sessions on GPU but can slightly increase CPU-side decoding overhead or cause small quality regressions for some prompts. We run comparative evals on your prompt set to recommend a quant profile; often we choose q4 for embeddings and q8 for chat-heavy generation as a balance.
[04:53] Mark Rivera: If we pick a quant profile, can we roll it out gradually? We need to measure quality regressions.
[04:58] Priya Nair: Yes — Redwood supports canary rollouts and traffic-split by model variant. You can route a percentage to quantized variant and monitor quality metrics. Our Optimize toolkit will surface regressions against a baseline eval set.
[05:10] Sofia Chen: For dedicated pools, what's the target CPU and networking per GPU? We're worried about network egress and NVLink saturation.
[05:18] Priya Nair: For NVLink heavy models we recommend racks with NVSwitch when possible. For networking, plan for at least 25-40Gbps per GPU for high-throughput workloads; CPU wise, ~4-8 vCPU per GPU for inference orchestration and batching. We'll include recommended instance types in the worksheet.
[05:33] Mark Rivera: Burst policies — can we set a hard budget for burst minutes per month to control cost?
[05:38] Jordan Lee: Yes, customers often set burst budgets. We support a few strategies: capped bursts (stop accepting burst beyond budget), pay-as-you-go bursts (billed at higher on-demand rate), or fallback to smaller low-cost variant models when burst budget exhausted.
[05:51] Alex Gomez: Fallback models — can those be different quant or smaller-arch models automatically?
[05:55] Priya Nair: Exactly. You can configure a fallback chain: same model quantized, then smaller distill model, then text-only summarizer as final fallback. Smart routing chooses based on latency and quality policy.
[06:07] Sofia Chen: For VPC/private deployment, how does autoscaling work when we operate on-prem? We can't spin up cloud GPUs instantly.
[06:14] Priya Nair: On-prem constraints mean we provide capacity planners that favor reserved pools with scheduled windows for expected spikes. For true elastic burst you'll need a hybrid approach — keep a small hot reserved pool on-prem and burst to cloud with secure peering, or provision enough reserved GPUs for worst-case within budget. We also support scheduled scale-ups (e.g., pre-warm before nightly report runs).
[06:33] Mark Rivera: Hybrid sounds promising but adds network egress and security questions.
[06:36] Jordan Lee: We'll include a VPC deployment diagram and network checklist; it covers peering, encrypted tunnels, egress estimates, and KMS integration.
[06:46] Alex Gomez: One operational question — queueing discipline and timeouts. If a request times out in the queue, do you return a retryable error code?
[06:53] Priya Nair: Yes we return distinct codes: 429 for rate limit, 503 with retryable header for transient capacity queueing, and an explicit ‘burst-budget-exhausted’ meta if you configured hard caps. The SDK surfaces these so your client can implement backoff or degrade gracefully.
[07:08] Sofia Chen: Can we see historical cost vs latency tradeoffs per route so execs can decide on reserved vs payg?
[07:12] Jordan Lee: Redwood Console has token-level cost breakdowns per route and model, and a cost vs latency simulation in Optimize. We'll share a demo link in the follow-up.
[07:22] Mark Rivera: About benchmarks — we'd like Redwood to run a 2-hour benchmark using our prompt set at our observed traffic patterns. Can you outline what you need from us?
[07:30] Priya Nair: We'll need three things: representative prompt set, token distribution (input/output), and a traffic pattern (rps over time). Also desired SLOs and any session affinity requirements. We'll schedule the run — usually we do a dedicated 4-GPU pool for 2 hours for a baseline.
[07:44] Alex Gomez: We'll share prompts and also a short script to emulate session stickiness.
[07:48] Jordan Lee: Great. We'll coordinate offline on timing, and Priya will prepare infra checklist.
[07:53] Priya Nair: Quick note about observability during benchmarks — we emit per-token latencies, KV cache hit rates, batch sizes, and queue lengths. That lets you see where bottlenecks are.
[08:03] Mark Rivera: One more thing: security/compliance. We need SOC2 and audit logs for requests.
[08:08] Jordan Lee: We'll share the SOC2 pack and our logging config; Dedicated and Private give you customer-visible audit logs and KMS-based key management.
[08:16] Sofia Chen: Cost question again: for reserved GPUs, is pricing monthly per GPU, and is there a commitment discount?
[08:22] Jordan Lee: Yes it's monthly reserved capacity with commit tiers — annual or monthly. We'll include pricing scenarios in the worksheet with example burst vs reserved mixes.
[08:30] Alex Gomez: Does Redwood support autoscaling cooldowns to avoid flapping?
[08:34] Priya Nair: Yes configurable cooldowns, and we use adaptive smoothing on scaling signals to avoid thrash. Also burst pre-warm windows can be scheduled to help known spikes.
[08:44] Mark Rivera: This was very helpful. Let's recap next steps.
[08:47] Jordan Lee: Recap: 1) We'll send capacity planning worksheet and recommended instance types. 2) Priya will own benchmark run plan and infra checklist. 3) Alex will share prompt set and traffic profile. 4) We'll share SOC2/security docs and VPC diagram. 5) Schedule the 2-hour benchmark and provide trial access to a 4-GPU dedicated pool.
[09:07] Sofia Chen: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[09:10] Alex Gomez: None from me, thanks.
[09:12] Priya Nair: Cool, we'll follow up quickly. Thanks everyone.
